nodes.label: dead-drop transport-agnostic runtime
nodes.rationale: Applications on different machines talk through infrastructure they already share (git repo, synced folder, object storage) so neither side must listen on a public port.

nodes.label: Two-package npm workspace
nodes.rationale: TypeScript throughout with zero runtime dependencies outside the workspace; layers are directories rather than packages so layering is enforced by lint rather than package boundaries.

nodes.label: npm run verify (the gate)
nodes.rationale: Lint, build and tests with coverage thresholds must pass before a change is done; CI additionally runs format:check, the three examples and the whole suite on Windows, so passing only on macOS is not finished.

nodes.label: git binary required, no network or credentials
nodes.norm_label: git binary required, no network or credentials

nodes.label: packages/transport-sdk
nodes.rationale: The contract third parties compile against, plus the conformance suite; versioned independently so an adapter written today keeps working across dead-drop majors.

nodes.label: protocol layer
nodes.rationale: Defines what a message is (envelope, framing, encryption, chunking, errors) and holds zero policy, so policy churn cannot break the wire contract.

nodes.label: core layer
nodes.rationale: All policy lives here: mailbox engine, transport manager, retry, breaker, dedupe, observability.

nodes.label: runtime layer
nodes.rationale: Workspaces, exposures, discovery, plugin loading, control plane.

nodes.label: sdk layer
nodes.rationale: Client over the control socket.

nodes.label: Tests mirror src, never live in src
nodes.rationale: Every layering rule scopes itself to src/, so keeping tests out of src/ is what makes tests exempt from layering restrictions.
nodes.norm_label: tests mirror src, never live in src

nodes.label: e2e scenario suite (run.sh, lib.sh, fast/ and live/)
nodes.norm_label: e2e scenario suite (run.sh, lib.sh, fast/ and live/)

nodes.label: docs/adr decision records
nodes.rationale: Anything that deviates from docs/vision.md gets a record explaining what was rejected and why.

nodes.label: Layering enforced by no-restricted-imports
nodes.rationale: Direction is protocol <- core <- runtime <- {sdk, cli}, enforced by eslint inside one package rather than by package boundaries. Two documented exceptions: runtime/plugins.ts owns the transport table, and the github transport delegates to git.

nodes.label: Invariant 1: nothing above the transport manager may name a transport
nodes.rationale: If application code could ask for 'the GitHub one', transport independence would be a slogan rather than a property.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 1: nothing above the transport manager may name a transport

nodes.label: Invariant 2: two transport kinds, store and native
nodes.rationale: Adapters implement put/get/list/delete (store) or send/subscribe (native); adding send/receive to the store contract is forbidden. See ADR 0001.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 2: two transport kinds, store and native

nodes.label: Invariant 3: control plane is a Unix socket mode 0600 or a Windows named pipe, never TCP
nodes.rationale: See ADR 0003; a TCP control plane would expose runtime control beyond local filesystem permissions.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 3: control plane is a unix socket mode 0600 or a windows named pipe, never tcp

nodes.label: Invariant 4: at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering per recipient
nodes.rationale: No doc or comment may claim a stronger guarantee than the system actually provides.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 4: at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering per recipient

nodes.label: Invariant 5: a message id is its trace id
nodes.rationale: workspace.request, mailbox.send and mailbox.deliver key their span to the envelope id, a response using its correlationId, which is what makes `ddrop trace <requestId>` work with the id a timeout error already returns.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 5: a message id is its trace id

nodes.label: Invariant 6: built-in transports may import only node builtins or declared dependencies
nodes.rationale: Workspaces are hoisted, so a module that loads in this repo can be missing from a real install. Enforced by test/transport-imports.test.ts; it went unguarded for several releases because the enforcing test was named after packages/cli and did not survive the consolidation.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 6: built-in transports may import only node builtins or declared dependencies

nodes.label: Invariant 7: transport-sdk is the only stable public contract
nodes.rationale: It is the one thing outside this repository that must keep working across releases, so changing it is a breaking change.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 7: transport-sdk is the only stable public contract

nodes.label: Invariant 8: never reintroduce the name Bridge
nodes.rationale: The old `bridge` binary collided with iproute2's bridge(8) on Linux. Checked with an rg command that must print nothing; only AGENTS.md and the release checklist may contain the word because they state the rule.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 8: never reintroduce the name bridge

nodes.label: Invariant 9: the transport is hostile storage for frame contents
nodes.rationale: Every frame is ciphertext including the envelope header, so no envelope field may leak a channel, peer or workspace name in clear text. Object keys are the deliberate exception so an operator can look at a git repo and understand it; a 0.1.0 release note claimed names never appear in clear text and was simply false.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 9: the transport is hostile storage for frame contents

nodes.label: Invariant 10: DeadDropError identity is a registry symbol, never instanceof
nodes.rationale: DeadDropError.is brand-checks Symbol.for('@fyrlabs/dead-drop.DeadDropError') so it holds when two copies of transport-sdk land in one dependency tree. With instanceof, a third-party adapter's non-retryable error would be re-wrapped by DeadDropError.from as INTERNAL, which is retryable, and the retry loop would hammer a permanent failure. The same reasoning forbids an exact-version pin on transport-sdk.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 10: deaddroperror identity is a registry symbol, never instanceof

nodes.label: Angular commit convention
nodes.rationale: type(scope): subject, imperative and lowercase, no trailing period; body explains what and why, not how; breaking changes use ! or a BREAKING CHANGE footer; one commit per completed logical unit, not one per session.

nodes.label: A test that would have caught the bug beats a test that covers the fix
nodes.rationale: Three real defects were caught this way and each is noted in the commit that fixed it. Coverage thresholds are 80% and sit near 90%, but coverage is a floor, not a goal.
nodes.norm_label: a test that would have caught the bug beats a test that covers the fix

nodes.label: Injected Clock, never Date.now or bare timers
nodes.rationale: The injected clock lets retry and backoff suites run in milliseconds instead of sleeping.
nodes.norm_label: injected clock, never date.now or bare timers

nodes.label: DeadDropError with stable code and honest retryable flag
nodes.rationale: The transport manager reads `retryable` to decide between retrying and failing over, so getting the flag wrong causes real misbehaviour.
nodes.norm_label: deaddroperror with stable code and honest retryable flag

nodes.label: Docs change in the same commit as behaviour
nodes.rationale: docs/configuration.md is expected to match runtime/config.ts field for field, and anything user-visible gets a CHANGELOG entry under Unreleased.
nodes.norm_label: docs change in the same commit as behaviour

nodes.label: Windows path and named-pipe trap
nodes.rationale: Never compare a resolved path against an unresolved one and never assume / separators. Two Windows-only CI failures happened here; the second was in a test whose helper bound its own control socket without taking the named-pipe branch defaultSocketPath takes, because listen on a socket path fails there with a bare EACCES that names nothing.

nodes.label: Workspace hoisting hides missing dependencies
nodes.rationale: Every workspace package resolves from the repo root, so check manifests, not just imports.

nodes.label: Renaming a symbol can reflow unrelated files
nodes.rationale: Identifier length changes reflow lines and fail format:check in untouched files, so run npm run format after any large rename.
nodes.norm_label: renaming a symbol can reflow unrelated files

nodes.label: npm bin path must not start with ./
nodes.rationale: A ./ prefix makes npm warn that the entry was invalid and removed; write dist/bin.js.
nodes.norm_label: npm bin path must not start with ./

nodes.label: defaultSocketPath and the 104-byte Unix socket cap
nodes.rationale: Past 104 bytes defaultSocketPath falls back to a hashed path under the temp directory; a raw join(dataDir, ...) is reachable from the documented quick start and bind fails with a bare EINVAL.
nodes.norm_label: defaultsocketpath and the 104-byte unix socket cap

nodes.label: git push exit 0 is not proof anything was published
nodes.rationale: push prints 'Everything up-to-date' and exits 0 when HEAD no longer carries the commit, which happens whenever a second process shares the clone, and ddrop connect starts its own runtime from the same config. The git transport checks merge-base --is-ancestor <commit> origin/<branch> instead; a live GitHub run lost 10 of 50 requests to the exit-code version.
nodes.norm_label: git push exit 0 is not proof anything was published

nodes.label: git rev-parse --git-dir answers for the enclosing repository
nodes.rationale: It exits 0 anywhere under a checkout, so using it to decide whether workDir is already this transport's clone made a nested workDir read the user's own project as the clone: initialise repointed origin, rewrote user.name/user.email and checked out an orphan branch over their work. Ask whether <workDir>/.git exists; a --show-toplevel path comparison also fails because the macOS temp directory is a symlink.
nodes.norm_label: git rev-parse --git-dir answers for the enclosing repository

nodes.label: A git working tree holds no dead-drop bookkeeping
nodes.rationale: git add --all stages everything under the prefix and walk lists everything that is not .git or README.md, so anything placed inside workDir is committed to the data branch and served as an object. The ownership lock and extra clones live beside workDir as <workDir>.owner and <workDir>.peers/; putting either inside broke checkout for every other clone twice.
nodes.norm_label: a git working tree holds no dead-drop bookkeeping

nodes.label: VERSION reads the package manifest, never a literal
nodes.rationale: A hard-coded literal in cli/cli.ts went stale and shipped a CLI reporting the wrong version in --version, status and /health. A test asserting CLI output equals VERSION does not catch it; assert against package.json.
nodes.norm_label: version reads the package manifest, never a literal

nodes.label: The two packages do not share a version
nodes.rationale: transport-sdk is the stable contract and moves rarely; @fyrlabs/dead-drop depends on it by caret range and churns freely. The release workflow skips whichever package is already on the registry at its manifest version, and the tag name tracks @fyrlabs/dead-drop.
nodes.norm_label: the two packages do not share a version

nodes.label: Never pin transport-sdk to an exact version
nodes.rationale: DeadDropError identity depends on one copy of transport-sdk being installed, and an exact pin forces a second copy into any tree that also holds a third-party adapter.
nodes.norm_label: never pin transport-sdk to an exact version

nodes.label: Releasing does not need permission
nodes.rationale: Version numbers are cheap; a broken artifact on the registry is not, because a published version can never be reused. Publish verified work rather than leaving it waiting to be asked about.

nodes.label: A tag is not a release
nodes.rationale: release.yml publishes when a GitHub release is published, so tags are cheap and reversible: pushing vX.Y.Z marks a candidate, gh release create is what puts it on npm, and a bad candidate is simply never released.
nodes.norm_label: a tag is not a release

nodes.label: Live GitHub walkthrough before tagging
nodes.rationale: Everything GitHub-specific is otherwise tested only against a scripted fake gh.

nodes.label: Throwaway private GitHub repos for testing
nodes.rationale: Fine to create without asking and to leave behind; deleting them needs a delete_repo scope that is deliberately not granted, which is why e2e/run.sh live takes the repository as an argument.
nodes.norm_label: throwaway private github repos for testing

nodes.label: AGENTS.md as the single source of repository instructions
nodes.rationale: Kept as one file so guidance cannot drift between tools; nothing repository-specific belongs in CLAUDE.md.
nodes.norm_label: agents.md as the single source of repository instructions

nodes.label: Tests prove behaviour, not coverage
nodes.rationale: A test that would not have caught a real defect is not worth the maintenance; the suite already caught three genuine bugs and that is the bar.

nodes.label: Comments explain why, never what
nodes.rationale: The code says what it does; a comment earns its place by recording a decision, a constraint or a trap.

nodes.label: Errors say what to do next
nodes.rationale: 'no config file found (looked in ...). Run "ddrop init" to create one.' beats a bare ENOENT.
nodes.norm_label: errors say what to do next

nodes.label: Nothing secret reaches a log
nodes.rationale: The logger redacts by field name and value pattern, but redaction is a backstop, not a licence to log freely.

nodes.label: No dependencies without a strong reason
nodes.rationale: The runtime holds credentials, so every dependency is supply-chain surface; the project has zero runtime dependencies outside its own packages and that is worth defending.
nodes.norm_label: no dependencies without a strong reason

nodes.label: PROTOCOL_VERSION and wire compatibility
nodes.rationale: The protocol is a wire contract between machines that may run different versions, so any change to the envelope, frame layout or error codes is a compatibility question first; bump PROTOCOL_VERSION and state how mixed-version peers behave.

nodes.label: Transport SDK changes are additive only
nodes.rationale: Packages outside this repository compile against it; a non-additive change needs a version bump and a migration note, and a new capability must gate its conformance tests so existing adapters keep passing.
nodes.norm_label: transport sdk changes are additive only

nodes.label: Transports are published outside this repository
nodes.rationale: Publish as <scope>/deaddrop-transport-<name>; transports living outside this repository is the design working, not a gap in it.
nodes.norm_label: transports are published outside this repository

nodes.label: Talking through already-shared infrastructure
nodes.rationale: Neither machine listens on a public port, so it works from behind NAT, from a CI runner, or from a locked-down corporate network.

nodes.label: One 32-byte workspace secret
nodes.rationale: Holding the secret is membership in the workspace, so it must travel over a trusted channel; passing it as --secret ddk1_... warns because an argument is visible in shell history and the process list.

nodes.label: AES-256-GCM over the whole frame including the envelope header
nodes.norm_label: aes-256-gcm over the whole frame including the envelope header

nodes.label: Object key layout ws/<workspace>/inbox/<peer>/<id>.ddf
nodes.rationale: A deliberate exception to encryption: anyone reading the transport sees workspace names, peer names and rough traffic volume, because an operator looking at a git repository should be able to tell what it holds. Message sizes and timing are visible for the same reason.

nodes.label: ddrop init
nodes.rationale: Writes a config and a secret beside it; --root points at a folder, --github at a repo, and --secret - joins an existing workspace by reading the secret from stdin so nothing has to be copied into place.

nodes.label: ddrop start
nodes.rationale: Runs in the foreground; backgrounding needs `exec`, otherwise kill reaps the wrapper shell and leaves the runtime serving.

nodes.label: ddrop expose
nodes.rationale: Exposes a directory or a local server and prints the exact command the other side runs, so you never have to look up your own peer id.

nodes.label: ddrop connect
nodes.rationale: Prints an ordinary local URL so nothing on that side knows the traffic crossed a transport.

nodes.label: ddrop keygen
nodes.rationale: Generates a new workspace secret for rotation.

nodes.label: --json output and runtime discovery through config
nodes.rationale: Client commands find the runtime through the config they discover, so they run from the directory holding deaddrop.config.json or take --config or --socket.
nodes.norm_label: --json output and runtime discovery through config

nodes.label: git transport
nodes.rationale: Data moves by pushing and pulling a dedicated orphan branch so the repository's real history is untouched.

nodes.label: github transport
nodes.rationale: Authentication is whatever gh already has, so dead-drop never sees a token; the repository is created private by default if it does not exist.

nodes.label: deaddrop-data orphan branch
nodes.rationale: Deleting that branch discards undelivered messages and nothing else.

nodes.label: memory transport
nodes.rationale: For tests and examples.

nodes.label: Transport policy: failover mode
nodes.rationale: A primary and a fallback list: when the LAN folder is unmounted the runtime works out it is gone and moves traffic to GitHub with no restart, so the caller sees a slow request rather than an error.

nodes.label: Transport policy: parallel mode
nodes.rationale: For peers that cannot all reach the same transports: every message goes to every transport and the recipient takes whichever copy arrives first, at the cost of a write per transport per message.

nodes.label: Every peer polls all the transports it has
nodes.rationale: Writes go to one transport, so a message written over a transport somebody else has not configured is a message that peer never receives; give every peer the same list.
nodes.norm_label: every peer polls all the transports it has

nodes.label: Not a message broker
nodes.rationale: A round trip over a git remote costs seconds, not milliseconds; if you have Kafka, use Kafka.

nodes.label: Keep a Changelog and semantic versioning
nodes.rationale: Versions track @fyrlabs/dead-drop; transport-sdk versions independently and its changes are called out explicitly.
nodes.norm_label: keep a changelog and semantic versioning

nodes.label: expose prints the peer's connect command (0.12.0)
nodes.rationale: Finding your own peer id used to be a separate command you had to know about; a directory now names the exposure after itself, while --target still needs --name because a url has no obvious name in it.
nodes.norm_label: expose prints the peer's connect command (0.12.0)

nodes.label: polling and policy validated at config load (0.12.0)
nodes.rationale: An unknown key, a number written as a string, a policy.primary that is not a name or a polling minimum above its maximum used to be accepted and then quietly do nothing; each now stops start-up with the field named.
nodes.norm_label: polling and policy validated at config load (0.12.0)

nodes.label: parallel policy actually fans out (0.11.0)
nodes.rationale: It used to be accepted and then quietly ignored, picking one transport like the default mode, so nobody who set it ever got a second copy.

nodes.label: inboxOrphanMs orphan mail reaping (0.10.0)
nodes.rationale: Only the addressed peer empties its inbox, so mail for a peer that never returns was unreclaimable storage (one trial repo squashed to a single commit still held 60 MB). Any peer now deletes such a message once it is older than 7 days AND its recipient has stopped publishing a presence beacon, so a peer merely offline for days keeps its mail.

nodes.label: compactAfterCommits data-branch compaction (0.8.0)
nodes.rationale: Every message left a commit behind for good, so joining a long-lived workspace kept getting slower. Past 500 commits whichever peer notices first replaces the branch with a single commit; turn it off where the branch is protected against force-pushes, and note compaction discards the commit log.

nodes.label: ddrop dashboard on 127.0.0.1:7373 (0.7.0)
nodes.rationale: Read-only, starts no runtime, reads the same control socket ddrop status does, and ships its page inside the package so it renders with no network. Anything with local access can read workspace metadata from the port, so run it while looking at it rather than as a service.

nodes.label: ddrop queues reads object keys only (0.6.0)
nodes.rationale: Nothing is decrypted and nothing is consumed, so you can see a peer that has stopped keeping up without waiting for a request to time out.
nodes.norm_label: ddrop queues reads object keys only (0.6.0)

nodes.label: discover distinguishes unreachable from empty (0.6.0)
nodes.rationale: It used to say 'No peers have announced themselves yet' and exit 0 when it could not reach any transport, so an unreachable workspace looked like an empty one.

nodes.label: transport-sdk 1.1.0 nested prefix listing check
nodes.rationale: A third-party adapter that listed only direct children would have reported every queue as empty.

nodes.label: workspace concurrency setting (0.5.0)
nodes.rationale: Default 1; raising it removes head-of-line blocking behind a slow handler at the cost of answering messages out of send order.

nodes.label: healthIntervalMs (0.5.0)
nodes.rationale: Default 30000; lower where probing is cheap, raise for github where every sweep spends an API call.

nodes.label: presenceIntervalMs (0.5.0)
nodes.rationale: Default 30000 leaves discovery up to 90 seconds stale; lower on a shared folder, leave alone on git where every beacon is a commit.

nodes.label: retry and breaker configurable (0.4.1)
nodes.rationale: Raising retry.maxAttempts alone usually buys nothing because since 0.3.0 the request timeout bounds the whole request, so extra attempts are cut off by the deadline; raise requestTimeoutMs with it.

nodes.label: init writes a config that works (0.4.0)
nodes.rationale: It generates the secret into .deaddrop/secret, writes the peer id explicitly so two peers no longer default to the same hostname and collide, and marks the shared location REPLACE-ME instead of quietly defaulting to a local folder that two people could never share.
nodes.norm_label: init writes a config that works (0.4.0)

nodes.label: ${file:PATH} and ${env:NAME} config interpolation (0.4.0)
nodes.rationale: Relative paths resolve against the config file and whitespace is stripped, so a config can be committed with the secret beside it rather than inside it.

nodes.label: Correction of the 'never in clear text' claim (0.2.3, 0.4.0)
nodes.rationale: The 0.1.0 notes and the README claimed channel, peer and workspace names never appear in clear text while listing object keys as unprotected two paragraphs later; keys carry those names deliberately, so the claim was corrected along with AGENTS.md invariant 9.
nodes.norm_label: correction of the 'never in clear text' claim (0.2.3, 0.4.0)

nodes.label: git transport no longer takes over an enclosing repository (0.3.1)
nodes.rationale: The quick start invited a relative workDir inside one of your own checkouts, and the transport then repointed origin, rewrote the commit name and email, and checked out its data branch over your work.
nodes.norm_label: git transport no longer takes over an enclosing repository (0.3.1)

nodes.label: Runtime starts even when no transport is reachable (0.3.1)
nodes.rationale: ddrop connect used to wait for the first presence beacon before binding its local port, so during an outage callers saw connection refused with nothing in the log.
nodes.norm_label: runtime starts even when no transport is reachable (0.3.1)

nodes.label: Presence beacons no longer pile up on a slow transport (0.3.1)
nodes.rationale: Only one is published at a time and it is abandoned once too old to be believed, so a merely slow backend is not pushed into failing by its own presence records.
nodes.norm_label: presence beacons no longer pile up on a slow transport (0.3.1)

nodes.label: A transport that failed to start once can recover (0.3.1)
nodes.rationale: The git and GitHub transports cached the first clone or auth failure and re-threw it for the life of the process, so a momentary network fault left a transport that could never recover whatever its breaker did.
nodes.norm_label: a transport that failed to start once can recover (0.3.1)

nodes.label: Request timeout bounds the whole request (0.3.0)
nodes.rationale: It used to guard only the wait for a reply, so a caller asking for 15 seconds could wait two minutes while transports failed; a transport legitimately slower than the deadline now fails at it instead of succeeding late.
nodes.norm_label: request timeout bounds the whole request (0.3.0)

nodes.label: Failover no longer backs off in front of an open breaker (0.3.0)
nodes.rationale: The manager moves to the next transport immediately, which is why the fallback was configured; failover takes seconds instead of minutes.
nodes.norm_label: failover no longer backs off in front of an open breaker (0.3.0)

nodes.label: allowPeers matches the caller's configured peerId (0.3.0)
nodes.rationale: It used to match the reply address, a per-process value for a ddrop connect client that appears in no config file, so a hand-written list matched nobody and denied everyone.
nodes.norm_label: allowpeers matches the caller's configured peerid (0.3.0)

nodes.label: Peer id split into mailbox address and identity (0.3.0)
nodes.rationale: One id was doing two jobs; separating them lets a short-lived session take its own address without losing who it is.
nodes.norm_label: peer id split into mailbox address and identity (0.3.0)

nodes.label: Timeout during an in-flight send no longer crashes the runtime (0.2.6)
nodes.norm_label: timeout during an in-flight send no longer crashes the runtime (0.2.6)

nodes.label: Missing exposure returns NOT_FOUND 404 instead of DECODE_FAILED 500 (0.2.6)
nodes.norm_label: missing exposure returns not_found 404 instead of decode_failed 500 (0.2.6)

nodes.label: Two-tier e2e suite: fast and live (0.2.6)
nodes.rationale: Every scenario states what a user can and cannot do; it first covered broadcast, key rotation, transport failover, message expiry, allowPeers and the http exposure type, and writing it produced two of the release's fixes.
nodes.norm_label: two-tier e2e suite: fast and live (0.2.6)

nodes.label: Second runtime clones into <workDir>.peers/ (0.2.5)
nodes.rationale: Two runtimes cannot share one git working tree, which git does not support; the first to start claims the directory, abandoned clones are removed at next start, and this mainly affects ddrop connect, which builds its runtime from the same config file.

nodes.label: A push counts as published only once the commit is on the remote-tracking branch (0.2.4)
nodes.rationale: git push exits 0 saying 'Everything up-to-date' when its commit is no longer HEAD, which happens whenever a second process shares the clone; a live GitHub run lost 10 of 50 requests to this.
nodes.norm_label: a push counts as published only once the commit is on the remote-tracking branch (0.2.4)

nodes.label: Non-retryable health failures logged at error level (0.2.3)
nodes.rationale: A wrong repo let the runtime report 'runtime started' and flap its breaker forever while the transport's own actionable message reached no log at any level.
nodes.norm_label: non-retryable health failures logged at error level (0.2.3)

nodes.label: Version read from the package manifest (0.2.1, 0.2.2)
nodes.rationale: A hard-coded literal reported 0.1.0 from a 0.2.0 install and fed the runtime, so ddrop status and /health reported it too; a test now fails the build if any source file hard-codes one.
nodes.norm_label: version read from the package manifest (0.2.1, 0.2.2)

nodes.label: Hashed short socket path under temp (0.2.1)
nodes.rationale: A Unix socket path cannot exceed 104 bytes and init writes a relative .deaddrop resolved against the working directory, so any project deeper than about 84 characters hit listen EINVAL. Runtime and client commands derive the fallback the same way, so discovery is unaffected.
nodes.norm_label: hashed short socket path under temp (0.2.1)

nodes.label: Consolidation from ten packages to two (0.2.0, breaking)
nodes.rationale: Everything except the transport contract lives in @fyrlabs/dead-drop reachable by subpath; transport-sdk stays separate so a third-party adapter does not depend on the whole runtime.
nodes.norm_label: consolidation from ten packages to two (0.2.0, breaking)

nodes.label: Error model moved into transport-sdk (0.2.0, breaking)
nodes.rationale: A transport adapter has to throw DeadDropError and the transport manager reads its retryable flag, so the error model belongs in the contract; the protocol layer re-exports it for compatibility.
nodes.norm_label: error model moved into transport-sdk (0.2.0, breaking)

nodes.label: DeadDropError.is brand-checks Symbol.for (0.2.0)
nodes.rationale: Previously an error crossing two copies of transport-sdk was re-wrapped as INTERNAL, which is retryable, so a permanent failure like UNAUTHORIZED would be retried indefinitely.

nodes.label: Built-in transports load through static import() thunks (0.2.0)
nodes.rationale: A dynamic import(variable) cannot be resolved relative to the importing module by bundlers or test runners, so the previous specifier-string form worked under plain Node and failed everywhere else.
nodes.norm_label: built-in transports load through static import() thunks (0.2.0)

nodes.label: Release workflow skips an already-published package (0.2.0)
nodes.rationale: It used to abort the whole job before the package that did change got published.
nodes.norm_label: release workflow skips an already-published package (0.2.0)

nodes.label: eslint no-restricted-imports replaced package-boundary layering (0.2.0)
nodes.rationale: Same direction inside one package: protocol imports nothing above it, core never names a transport, and a transport sees only the protocol and the transport SDK.

nodes.label: At-least-once delivery machinery over plain object storage (0.1.0)
nodes.rationale: Framing, chunking, delete-as-acknowledgement, redelivery with backoff, dead letters, deduplication, retained broadcast topics, and polling that adapts to traffic.
nodes.norm_label: at-least-once delivery machinery over plain object storage (0.1.0)

nodes.label: Proxy mode (0.1.0)
nodes.rationale: expose --target makes an unmodified local server reachable to peers and connect serves it back as an ordinary local URL; static directory exposures too.

nodes.label: Observability: JSON logs with redaction, Prometheus metrics, tracing (0.1.0)
nodes.rationale: A message id is its own trace id, so ddrop trace <requestId> works with the id a timeout error already returns.
nodes.norm_label: observability: json logs with redaction, prometheus metrics, tracing (0.1.0)

nodes.label: Multiple transports with health scoring, jittered retry, breaking and failover (0.1.0)
nodes.norm_label: multiple transports with health scoring, jittered retry, breaking and failover (0.1.0)

nodes.label: Plugin contract and framework-agnostic conformance suite (0.1.0)
nodes.rationale: A store adapter is four methods.
nodes.norm_label: plugin contract and framework-agnostic conformance suite (0.1.0)

nodes.label: Responses buffered whole and capped at 32 MiB
nodes.rationale: Streaming is not implemented.
nodes.norm_label: responses buffered whole and capped at 32 mib

nodes.label: Duplicates are suppressed, not prevented
nodes.rationale: Ordering is best-effort per recipient, so handlers must be safe to run twice.

nodes.label: docs/architecture.md
nodes.rationale: Read before changing anything structural: it explains the layering and what each layer is forbidden to know.

nodes.label: ADR 0001: two transport kinds instead of one interface
nodes.rationale: Status accepted. Splits the transport contract by what a backend actually provides, because every intended backend (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, OneDrive, SharePoint, filesystem, S3, Dropbox) is an object store with no delivery semantics.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0001: two transport kinds instead of one interface

nodes.label: Original single Transport interface (connect/send/receive/health/close)
nodes.rationale: The design sketch's uniform interface. Rejected because send/receive asks each adapter to invent messaging on top of storage.

nodes.label: Reinvented delivery semantics per adapter
nodes.rationale: Implementing receive against a store forces polling with adaptive backoff, acknowledgement, deduplication, redelivery with jitter, dead-lettering and chunking for the 100 MB blob limit, rewritten by every adapter author. Consequences: adapters become several hundred lines so fewer get written, each carries its own delivery bugs in a package this repo does not control, and the cost of entry undermines the open plugin ecosystem goal.

nodes.label: capabilities.kind === 'store'
nodes.rationale: put / get / list / delete, optional watch. Four methods is the whole adapter surface, which keeps the conformance suite strict and adapters small.

nodes.label: capabilities.kind === 'native'
nodes.rationale: send / subscribe. Kept for backends that genuinely are message systems, where synthesising acknowledgements on top of them would be wrong.

nodes.label: Mailbox engine in @fyrlabs/dead-drop/core
nodes.rationale: Implements messaging once over the store primitives so delivery correctness is implemented once, tested once and fixed once. Cost: the runtime does more work, so its bugs affect every transport, mitigated by it being the most heavily tested code in the repository.

nodes.label: Delete-as-acknowledgement
nodes.rationale: Acknowledgement is modelled as deleting the object, which is the only primitive a store offers; the side effect is that no record of a finished job survives.

nodes.label: Chunking and reassembly
nodes.rationale: Needed because stores impose blob size limits such as GitHub's 100 MB; done once in the engine rather than per adapter.

nodes.label: Redelivery with backoff
nodes.rationale: Automatic redelivery lives in the engine, which is why request-level retry is not exposed as a user-facing control.

nodes.label: Dead letters
nodes.rationale: Terminal destination for messages that exhaust redelivery, implemented once in the engine.

nodes.label: Deduplication
nodes.rationale: Store-backed delivery is at-least-once, so the engine dedupes rather than each adapter.

nodes.label: Broadcast topics with a resume cursor
nodes.rationale: Fan-out reads cannot use delete-as-acknowledgement, so subscribers track position with a cursor instead.
nodes.norm_label: broadcast topics with a resume cursor

nodes.label: Adaptive polling
nodes.rationale: Stores have no push, and only optional watch, so the engine polls with adaptive backoff instead of requiring adapters to.

nodes.label: StoreBackedTransport base class (rejected alternative)
nodes.rationale: Keep the single interface and ship a base class adapters extend. Rejected because inheritance across a package boundary is a versioning trap, and because it leaves the door open to adapters that half-implement delivery.

nodes.label: Open plugin ecosystem goal
nodes.rationale: The force driving the split: a several-hundred-line cost of entry per adapter undermines third-party transports, so the contract has to be small enough that a store adapter is four methods.

nodes.label: Intended backends are all object stores
nodes.rationale: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, OneDrive, SharePoint, local filesystem, S3-compatible storage and Dropbox are every one an object store with no delivery semantics, which is the observation the whole ADR turns on.
nodes.norm_label: intended backends are all object stores

nodes.label: Filesystem transport (~300 lines, atomic writes, polling watcher)
nodes.rationale: Cited as evidence the split works: a complete store adapter fits in about 300 lines including atomic writes and a polling watcher.
nodes.norm_label: filesystem transport (~300 lines, atomic writes, polling watcher)

nodes.label: ADR 0002: filesystem is the reference transport, not GitHub
nodes.rationale: Status accepted. Reverses the original sketch's plan to build GitHub first, because 'build one complete transport to validate the abstraction' only works if the validation is repeatable.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0002: filesystem is the reference transport, not github

nodes.label: Filesystem as the reference transport
nodes.rationale: Two runtimes pointed at one directory exercise the entire stack (encryption, chunking, acknowledgement, discovery, proxying) with no credentials and no network, so the full stack is verified on every commit by anyone in seconds. It is also independently useful: a shared mount, SMB share, Dropbox or OneDrive folder, or two runtimes on one machine.

nodes.label: GitHub cannot be tested in CI
nodes.rationale: Exercising GitHub needs a token, a repository, network access and an account, so CI cannot run it and a contributor cannot run it. The abstraction it was meant to validate would be validated by a suite nobody can execute.
nodes.norm_label: github cannot be tested in ci

nodes.label: End-to-end suite over two runtimes and one directory
nodes.rationale: Runs against the filesystem transport so the whole stack is covered without credentials or network.
nodes.norm_label: end-to-end suite over two runtimes and one directory

nodes.label: git transport (second transport)
nodes.rationale: Tested against a local bare repository, which is a real git remote, so clone, commit, push, fetch, reset and the push-race path are genuinely exercised with no network and no credentials.

nodes.label: Local bare repository test fixture
nodes.rationale: A real git remote without network or credentials, which is what makes the git and github transports testable at all.

nodes.label: Push-race path
nodes.rationale: Concurrent pushes to the shared data branch, exercised against the local bare repo rather than left to live-service luck.

nodes.label: GitHub transport as a thin layer over git
nodes.rationale: Adds only what is GitHub-specific: gh-based authentication, repository resolution and creation, and rate-limit reporting. Keeping it thin is what lets a scripted fake gh plus a local bare repo cover its logic.
nodes.norm_label: github transport as a thin layer over git

nodes.label: Scripted fake gh CLI
nodes.rationale: Substitutes for the live gh binary so GitHub-specific logic is testable offline.

nodes.label: Manual live-GitHub checklist in docs/testing.md
nodes.rationale: Real rate limits, real auth failures and real large-repo latency are only covered by a human running the checklist. Recorded explicitly rather than hidden behind a green tick.

nodes.label: ADR 0003: the control plane is a Unix socket, not localhost TCP
nodes.rationale: Status accepted. Chooses among the sketch's options (localhost HTTP, Unix domain socket, named pipe, platform IPC) on the grounds that the control plane is the door to every workspace secret.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0003: the control plane is a unix socket, not localhost tcp

nodes.label: Local runtime control plane
nodes.rationale: Anything that can reach it can publish to any channel, call any peer, read runtime status and add exposures. The capability behind the listener, not the listener's transport, is the threat.

nodes.label: Unix domain socket at mode 0600
nodes.rationale: A socket file is governed by filesystem permissions the OS already enforces and operators already understand; 0600 in the runtime's data directory means the owner and nobody else, and permissions are visible with ls -l.

nodes.label: Named pipe on Windows
nodes.rationale: Windows has no Unix socket, so path handling carries a platform branch. That branch is the accepted cost of never using TCP.

nodes.label: Localhost TCP control plane (rejected)
nodes.rationale: A 127.0.0.1 port is reachable by every process running as any user on the machine, by every container sharing the network namespace, and with a misconfigured Docker port publish or a 0.0.0.0 bind from outside.

nodes.label: Token authentication scheme (rejected)
nodes.rationale: No authentication step fixes a TCP control plane without inventing a token scheme, storing that token somewhere, and having every client find it. Avoiding it means nothing to design, distribute or leak.

nodes.label: Filesystem permissions as the access control mechanism
nodes.rationale: Reuse of an enforcement mechanism the operating system already provides and operators already read, instead of a bespoke authentication layer.
nodes.norm_label: filesystem permissions as the access control mechanism

nodes.label: Cross-container clients must mount the socket
nodes.rationale: A client in a different container cannot reach the runtime without mounting the socket, which is deliberate rather than an oversight.
nodes.norm_label: cross-container clients must mount the socket

nodes.label: Future opt-in networked listener
nodes.rationale: If a networked control plane is ever genuinely needed it must be a separate opt-in listener with real authentication, never a relaxation of the socket decision.

nodes.label: ADR 0004: ddrop dashboard binds a TCP port and is a control-socket client
nodes.rationale: Status accepted. Exists because a browser cannot open a Unix socket, so a dashboard appears to conflict head-on with ADR 0003 and invariant 3.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0004: ddrop dashboard binds a tcp port and is a control-socket client

nodes.label: ddrop dashboard command
nodes.rationale: Binds an HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 serving a static page plus a read-only JSON API, and reaches the runtime as a client of the control socket exactly as ddrop status does. It constructs no DeadDropRuntime, so only ddrop start and ddrop connect remain runtime constructors.

nodes.label: Read-only constraint on the dashboard API
nodes.rationale: No route publishes, calls, exposes, cancels or retries, and the socket's write routes (/publish, /call, /expose) are not proxied. Read-only is what preserves the argument that the browser user already holds this capability by being able to run ddrop status, so it is a constraint of the decision and not a first-release simplification.
nodes.norm_label: read-only constraint on the dashboard api

nodes.label: Dashboard as another control-socket consumer
nodes.rationale: The control plane is unchanged: still a socket at mode 0600, with the dashboard in the same category as ddrop status, ddrop discover and ddrop logs. Nothing about the runtime's listener moves.

nodes.label: Structured control-plane data (/peers, /transports, /status, /queues, logs, traces, metrics)
nodes.rationale: Everything a read-only dashboard would show already exists here, which is why the dashboard needs no runtime of its own and can show nothing the control plane does not already return.
nodes.norm_label: structured control-plane data (/peers, /transports, /status, /queues, logs, traces, metrics)

nodes.label: Explicit 127.0.0.1 bind, never 0.0.0.0
nodes.rationale: The port is a view of data the operator can already read in their own terminal, held open by a foreground process that exits when they stop it.

nodes.label: Browser-reachable localhost threat (CSRF, Origin, DNS rebinding)
nodes.rationale: The decisive reason is narrower than 'TCP is riskier than a socket' and specific to browsers: any web page the user visits can issue requests at 127.0.0.1. Defending state-changing endpoints needs Origin validation, CSRF tokens and DNS-rebinding-resistant Host checks, each easy and collectively easy to get subtly wrong. When every endpoint only reads, the worst outcome degrades from an action taken to information disclosed.
nodes.norm_label: browser-reachable localhost threat (csrf, origin, dns rebinding)

nodes.label: A writable dashboard would reopen this ADR
nodes.rationale: A cancel or retry button is two stacked decisions: whether to build a job-control primitive at all (nothing in the runtime cancels a queued message today, and redelivery is already automatic), and whether to put it on a browser-reachable port. Keep them apart.
nodes.norm_label: a writable dashboard would reopen this adr

nodes.label: Request-level retry hazard under at-least-once delivery
nodes.rationale: Delivery is at-least-once and idempotencyKey dedupes per runtime only, so retrying onto a second worker runs the job twice with neither side able to notice, and no backend offers the compare-and-swap needed to fix that.
nodes.norm_label: request-level retry hazard under at-least-once delivery

nodes.label: Dashboard constructs no DeadDropRuntime
nodes.rationale: The second half of the decision matters more than the TCP question, because the tempting implementation (copy ddrop connect) is the wrong one. A dashboard that only reads needs no runtime, no workDir, no peer id and no beacons. The general rule the workDir bugs taught: dead-drop's own machinery must not entangle itself with the thing the user is sharing.

nodes.label: workDir ownership collision
nodes.rationale: A git working tree has one writer. The ownership lock added in 0.2.5 catches the second runtime and forces it into <workDir>.peers/, so every dashboard session would clone the whole data branch.

nodes.label: Phantom peers from ephemeral client identities
nodes.rationale: A runtime publishes presence beacons under an ephemeral <configured>-c<pid-hex> identity, so every dashboard session would appear in every peer's ddrop discover as a peer that answers nothing.
nodes.norm_label: phantom peers from ephemeral client identities

nodes.label: Unbounded beacon commits on git and github
nodes.rationale: On the git and github transports each beacon is a commit and a push, so a dashboard left open all day would write commits all day into a history that already grows without bound.
nodes.norm_label: unbounded beacon commits on git and github

nodes.label: Explicit --port with loud EADDRINUSE failure
nodes.rationale: Defaults to a port ddrop connect does not hand out and fails loudly rather than hunting for a free one, because a dashboard that silently moves is a dashboard nobody can bookmark.

nodes.label: Workspace metadata disclosure through the open port
nodes.rationale: Peer names, channel names, queue depths, and through logs and traces rather more, are readable by anything with local access while the port is open. The names are already in the clear in the store's object keys (invariant 9), but that store is readable by workspace members whereas this port is readable by any process on the machine and by content the user's browser loads. A smaller audience shift than a write capability, still a real one, so the port is loopback-bound, open only during the foreground command, and documented as carrying workspace metadata.
nodes.norm_label: workspace metadata disclosure through the open port

nodes.label: Opening a browser is a convenience, not a dependency
nodes.rationale: The URL is printed before the open is attempted, --no-open skips it, and a failed open never fails the command, because dead-drop runs on headless machines as an ordinary deployment where open fails or hangs.
nodes.norm_label: opening a browser is a convenience, not a dependency

nodes.label: Retention store for completed jobs (deferred)
nodes.rationale: 'Completed jobs and who requested them' cannot be shown because delivery is delete-as-acknowledgement and no record of a finished job survives. Keeping one changes what the runtime retains and therefore touches the security model, so it is a separate decision.

nodes.label: Serve the dashboard from the runtime itself (rejected)
nodes.rationale: The shortest path and the worst one: it puts a TCP listener on the process holding the secrets, exactly what ADR 0003 forbids, and makes every ddrop start a web server whether or not anyone wants one.
nodes.norm_label: serve the dashboard from the runtime itself (rejected)

nodes.label: Terminal UI ddrop top (rejected as a substitute)
nodes.rationale: Genuinely appealing, needs no port, still worth building on its own merits, but not a substitute: the ask was something to leave open on a second monitor and hand to someone who does not use the CLI.
nodes.norm_label: terminal ui ddrop top (rejected as a substitute)

nodes.label: Load the frontend library from a CDN (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Rejected on principle: the product exists to work through infrastructure you already have, sometimes offline, so a dashboard needing the internet to render contradicts it. The library is vendored into the CLI package's static assets, keeping it out of the dependency tree and leaving the zero-runtime-dependency claim intact.
nodes.norm_label: load the frontend library from a cdn (rejected)

nodes.label: Vendored static frontend assets in the CLI package
nodes.rationale: Vendoring keeps the frontend out of the dependency tree and preserves the zero-runtime-dependency claim while allowing offline rendering.
nodes.norm_label: vendored static frontend assets in the cli package

nodes.label: Invariant 3: control plane is a socket or named pipe, never TCP
nodes.rationale: The repository invariant that encodes ADR 0003 and that the dashboard appears to violate at a glance.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 3: control plane is a socket or named pipe, never tcp

nodes.label: Invariant 9: names are in the clear in store object keys
nodes.rationale: Peer and channel names are already visible to workspace members in object keys; the dashboard port widens the audience for that same metadata to any local process.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 9: names are in the clear in store object keys

nodes.label: ddrop connect (runtime constructor)
nodes.rationale: Builds a DeadDropRuntime from the user's config. Copying it into the dashboard would import all three of its collisions with whatever the user is sharing.

nodes.label: ddrop status (existing control-socket client)
nodes.rationale: The precedent the dashboard is modelled on, and the capability baseline the read-only argument rests on.

nodes.label: ADR 0005: compacting the data branch by re-orphaning under a lease
nodes.rationale: Status accepted. Git and github transports commit every mutation (195 commits for ~100 messages in two live runs), so the tree stays small but history grows forever. Two harms: joining costs more forever because initialise fetches every reachable object, and the repository grows without bound until it hits the host size limit and stops accepting pushes, which ends the workspace.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0005: compacting the data branch by re-orphaning under a lease

nodes.label: Compaction (re-orphaning the data branch)
nodes.rationale: Periodically replace the data branch with a single parentless commit holding the branch's current tree, published with a compare-and-swap force-push. Reusing the existing tree object means content is preserved bit for bit rather than rebuilt, so compaction cannot corrupt or drop a message by construction. Measured on a 201-commit history: 803 objects/588K/depth 201 uncompacted versus 10 objects/160K/depth 1 compacted, against a remote that had NOT been garbage collected, which is the only case that matters because no client can make GitHub run a gc.

nodes.label: The data branch
nodes.rationale: The git branch every mutation is committed to. A send is a commit, the response is a commit, and the delete that acknowledges delivery is a third.

nodes.label: git commit-tree (parentless commit)
nodes.rationale: commit-tree with no -p produces a commit with no parents, which is what makes the result an orphan. Three plumbing commands total, touching neither the working tree nor the index.

nodes.label: Explicit-value --force-with-lease=<branch>:<commit>
nodes.rationale: The lease must take an explicit expected value, never the bare --force-with-lease. The bare form leases against the remote-tracking ref, which sync() refreshes constantly; a poll landing between snapshot and push would silently update origin/<branch>, make the lease agree with itself, and turn the compare-and-swap into an unconditional force-push. This is the entire safety argument and must not be simplified away. Protect it with a test that would have caught its absence, not one that covers its presence.

nodes.label: Any peer may compact, no election
nodes.rationale: The lease makes concurrent attempts safe: one wins, the others are rejected against a tip already compacted by somebody else. A rejected compaction is not retried and not an error; it is logged at debug and dropped, because the work it wanted done is done.
nodes.norm_label: any peer may compact, no election

nodes.label: Flush lock serialisation of compaction
nodes.rationale: Compaction runs inside the existing flush lock, after a successful flush, so it cannot interleave with applyBatch in our own process. The flush lock is the mechanism that already serialises writes.

nodes.label: compactAfterCommits config field
nodes.rationale: Trigger is local history depth via git rev-list --count HEAD, a local read. Defaults to 500 with 0 to disable, keeping compaction roughly two orders of magnitude rarer than the pushRetries budget of 5 that absorbs its collisions.

nodes.label: pushRetries budget
nodes.rationale: Budget of 5 retries that absorbs collisions caused by compaction losing or winning a race.

nodes.label: Refused compaction waits a full threshold
nodes.rationale: A lost lease means somebody else is compacting; a branch protected against force-pushes will refuse the next attempt too. Without the floor, either case spends a wasted push on every flush, a throughput regression paid forever in exchange for nothing.
nodes.norm_label: refused compaction waits a full threshold

nodes.label: sync() fetch plus reset --hard
nodes.rationale: sync() is already git fetch origin <branch> followed by git reset --hard origin/<branch>, and a hard reset adopts an unrelated history as readily as a descendant one. The + in the refspec +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/* lets the non-fast-forward remote-tracking update through, so every peer picks up a rewritten branch through the code path it already runs every five seconds. This is why peers need no new code to survive compaction.

nodes.label: initialise (git init plus fetch)
nodes.rationale: Transfers every object reachable from the branch tip. Since the 0.2.5 working-tree ownership lock, a second runtime on one machine and every ddrop connect clone separately into <workDir>.peers/ and pay that cost again.

nodes.label: applyBatch replay loop
nodes.rationale: Treats a compaction it lost a race to exactly as any other lost race: reset to the remote, replay the batch, push again. Compaction adds a new cause for a code path that already exists, not a new code path.

nodes.label: isNonFastForward rejection matcher
nodes.rationale: Already matches both the 'stale info' and 'fetch first' rejection messages compaction produces.

nodes.label: ensureClone memoised-failure clearing
nodes.rationale: When a peer's fetch fails because the host stopped serving objects the branch no longer reaches, the error is retryable, ensureClone clears its memoised failure, and the next attempt succeeds against the new tip.

nodes.label: Two-peer lab verification of the four safety properties
nodes.rationale: Verified against real git rather than reasoned about, because the failure mode of getting this wrong is silent message loss, the exact class of defect that has already bitten this project twice. Results: tree preserved (depth 31 to 1, identical tree object, 30 of 30 messages); an existing peer recovered unaided through plain fetch plus reset --hard; a concurrent writer was protected (lease rejected with stale info); a peer mid-flush was rejected 'fetch first' and the existing replay loop re-pushed intact.
nodes.norm_label: two-peer lab verification of the four safety properties

nodes.label: Rejected: shallow fetch (--depth=1)
nodes.rationale: Not a strawman: tested and works, a shallow peer joined a 201-commit remote at 124K, pushed back successfully and stayed shallow across an ordinary sync, needing no force-push. Rejected as THE answer because it fixes only the join cost while the host repository still grows forever. Complementary rather than alternative, and it has an unmeasured tail: a shallow peer accumulates every commit made after it joined and drifts back unless it re-shallows.

nodes.label: Rejected: delete and recreate the branch
nodes.rationale: Strictly worse than a leased force-push: there is a window in which the branch does not exist, and any peer calling initialise in that window takes the create-orphan path and races to publish a competing branch.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: delete and recreate the branch

nodes.label: Rejected: epoch scheme (a branch per generation)
nodes.rationale: Solves the same problem with more moving parts, and every reader has to discover which epoch is current before it can read anything. The force-push is renamed into a branch deletion rather than avoided.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: epoch scheme (a branch per generation)

nodes.label: Rejected: rewriting history with filter-branch or filter-repo
nodes.rationale: Same force-push, same lease requirement, far slower, and pointless: nothing needs the intermediate commits rewritten, only discarded.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: rewriting history with filter-branch or filter-repo

nodes.label: Commit history as the only record a message existed
nodes.rationale: Delivery is delete-as-acknowledgement, so the data branch's commit log is the sole place a delivered message survives. Nothing reads it and no feature depends on it, so nothing breaks, but it forecloses an accidental audit trail. That supports the backlog position that an audit story needs designing deliberately: commit history is metadata the encryption exists to protect and should not become a feature by default. Also, git log stops being a hand-debugging tool for a workspace.
nodes.norm_label: commit history as the only record a message existed

nodes.label: Nobody's disk shrinks on its own
nodes.rationale: An existing peer keeps old objects until it runs git gc; measured, a peer sat at 3.7M and fell to 136K only after reflog expire --expire=now --all plus gc --prune=now. The host keeps them until its own gc, which cannot be triggered. Compaction fixes what a new peer pays, immediately, not what an old peer already holds.
nodes.norm_label: nobody's disk shrinks on its own

nodes.label: Compaction degrades gracefully
nodes.rationale: If the branch is force-push protected or the host refuses the lease, compaction fails, the failure is logged, messages keep flowing, and history keeps growing as today. It can never take a workspace down; it can only fail to help.

nodes.label: ADR 0006: any member may reap an orphaned inbox, on age plus absence
nodes.rationale: Status accepted, implemented in 0.10.0. Nothing ever deletes a message from a peer's inbox except that peer, so mail addressed to a peer that never comes back is unreachable garbage. Measured: after compacting a trial repository from 3,075 commits and 433 MB to a single commit, 60 MB survived for a live tree of 17 files, almost entirely two abandoned 30 MiB payloads in dead ephemeral peers' inboxes plus stale beacons.
nodes.norm_label: adr 0006: any member may reap an orphaned inbox, on age plus absence

nodes.label: Workspace.reap()
nodes.rationale: The reaper lives in Workspace beside queues(), reusing its listing and key parsing, so core stays pure mechanism and gains no dependency on the runtime. Eight guards, each confirmed by removing it and watching a named test fail.

nodes.label: Stale presence beacon reaper (aggressive)
nodes.rationale: Any peer deletes a beacon at ws/<workspace>/peers/<peer>.ddf whose announcedAt is older than a small multiple of presenceTtlMs. A beacon is self-healing: a live peer rewrites it every presenceIntervalMs (30s default), so deleting one wrongly costs at most one interval of invisibility to discover.

nodes.label: Orphaned inbox object reaper (conservative)
nodes.rationale: Deletes ws/<workspace>/inbox/<peer>/<id>.ddf only when all three hold: the peer is not this peer, the object is older than inboxOrphanMs, and the owning peer has no beacon at all or a beacon older than inboxOrphanMs. A message is not self-healing and deleting one wrongly is unrecoverable, so it gets a far longer horizon than a beacon; collapsing the two would either leak beacons for a week or destroy mail in minutes.

nodes.label: inboxOrphanMs horizon
nodes.rationale: Default 7 days, 0 disables and restores today's behaviour exactly. A backstop against abandonment, not an expiry mechanism; a message with no TTL at all is still subject to it. The 7 day default sits far beyond a closed laptop and far below forever. Clock skew between peers shifts the effective horizon by the skew, which at 7 days needs extraordinary skew to matter.

nodes.label: Age comes from the key, never the payload
nodes.rationale: parseInboxKey returns the message id and idTime decodes a creation timestamp from it. Cost: deciding by download would mean fetching every object in every inbox on every cycle, reading the entire leak in order to decide to delete it. Availability: modifiedAt is optional in the store contract and backend-dependent, while the id is the sender's own clock and always present. Same reasoning reapTopics already applies, from the 'age unknown is not old enough to delete' lesson.
nodes.norm_label: age comes from the key, never the payload

nodes.label: idTime / parseInboxKey
nodes.rationale: parseInboxKey returns the message id; idTime decodes a creation timestamp out of it. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is decrypted to make a reaping decision.

nodes.label: reapTopics (mailbox.ts:700)
nodes.rationale: Covers broadcast topics only, and already takes age from the id at mailbox.ts:716 for the same availability reasons.

nodes.label: core/mailbox.ts delivery loop
nodes.rationale: mailbox.ts:434 polls inboxPrefix(workspace, this.peerId), the peer's own inbox and nothing else. TTL expiry at mailbox.ts:548 fires inside that peer's own loop, so it never runs for a peer that is gone.

nodes.label: queues() diagnostic (runtime/workspace.ts:575)
nodes.rationale: The only caller that lists inboxRoot, the all-peers prefix, and it deletes nothing. reap() reuses its listing and key parsing.

nodes.label: isExpired / per-message TTL
nodes.rationale: isExpired reads ttlMs and ts from the envelope header, and that header is encrypted. Honouring a message's real TTL from outside its recipient would require decrypting every candidate, so orphan reaping is explicitly not TTL and must not be described as one.

nodes.label: Absence of a beacon as the liveness signal
nodes.rationale: stop() calls withdraw() (workspace.ts:290 and :844), which deletes the peer's own beacon, so a cleanly exited peer leaves no beacon and a populated inbox, which is exactly the measured case. A crashed peer leaves a beacon that stops being refreshed. 'No beacon, or one older than the horizon' covers both. Age alone would be wrong: a peer offline over a holiday has old messages and is not orphaned. Requiring both conditions separates 'gone' from 'not looking right now'.
nodes.norm_label: absence of a beacon as the liveness signal

nodes.label: discoverPeers({ includeStale: true }) / listBeacons
nodes.rationale: Already returns announce times for every beacon it can read. It skips beacons it cannot decode, which is why listBeacons returns the objects it found separately from the records it decoded.

nodes.label: A partial view is not a view
nodes.rationale: Absence of a beacon is the entire liveness signal, so a store that failed to answer is indistinguishable from a workspace where nobody is alive. The pass deletes nothing unless every store answered; without that, one transient outage on a multi-transport workspace clears every inbox.
nodes.norm_label: a partial view is not a view

nodes.label: An undecodable beacon still counts as liveness
nodes.rationale: Beacons that cannot be read belong to a key era this peer does not hold, and their owners may be perfectly alive, so the existence of the object is the signal and its contents are not required.
nodes.norm_label: an undecodable beacon still counts as liveness

nodes.label: A stale beacon is kept while its owner still has mail
nodes.rationale: A beacon goes stale in fifteen minutes and mail lives seven days, so the beacon reaper would routinely destroy the one piece of evidence telling the next pass that a backlog belongs to someone recently alive. The beacon follows on a later pass once the mail is reaped.
nodes.norm_label: a stale beacon is kept while its owner still has mail

nodes.label: Shared reaper throttle on the presence interval
nodes.rationale: The 'same poll cycle as reapTopics' idea was a MailboxEngine notion and the engine's poll is not visible from Workspace, so the pass rides the presence interval and carries its own throttle of ten presenceTtlMs, fifteen minutes at defaults. Cheap because on git and github a listing reads the working tree the mailbox poll already keeps fresh. The pass does not run during start(), since start-up had already moved the first beacon off its critical path and a full inbox listing is much heavier than one put.
nodes.norm_label: shared reaper throttle on the presence interval

nodes.label: Ephemeral <configured>-c<pid-hex> connect peers
nodes.rationale: Every ddrop connect runs its own runtime under an ephemeral identity, so each invocation can strand whatever was in flight when it exited. Measured culprits: peer-b-c2192 and peer-b-c14c9e.

nodes.label: Reaping grants no new privilege
nodes.rationale: Every member already holds the workspace secret and can fetch and decode any object in any inbox, and every member already has unrestricted delete because authorisation lives in the transport's access control, not in dead-drop. A hostile member can wipe every inbox today with no code from this ADR. What changes is that correct peers now delete data they did not author, so the risk to design against is accidental loss, not privilege escalation.

nodes.label: allowPeers guardrail
nodes.rationale: Documented in docs/security-model.md as a guardrail rather than a boundary, and it cannot be used with ddrop connect at all.

nodes.label: Invariant 9 (keys carry names in the clear by design)
nodes.rationale: Untouched by reaping: the reaper reads object keys, which already carry workspace and peer names by documented design, and decrypts nothing.
nodes.norm_label: invariant 9 (keys carry names in the clear by design)

nodes.label: Rejected: reaping by peer-id shape
nodes.rationale: Matching the <configured>-c<pid-hex> pattern identifies the measured culprit precisely and is still the wrong mechanism: it hard-codes a naming convention into a destructive operation and misses every orphan that did not come from connect.

nodes.label: Rejected: an owner or elected reaper
nodes.rationale: No election exists, ADR 0005 already set the precedent that any peer may perform maintenance when the operation itself is safe, and a single designated reaper is a single point of failure for a leak that only matters over months.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: an owner or elected reaper

nodes.label: Rejected: honouring real per-message TTL by decrypting candidates
nodes.rationale: Correct, and it costs a full download of everything under consideration on every cycle.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: honouring real per-message ttl by decrypting candidates

nodes.label: Rejected: sender-side expiry
nodes.rationale: By the time a message is orphaned the sender is usually gone too, since the common case is an ephemeral connect peer on both ends.

nodes.label: Rejected: doing nothing because compaction bounds the repository
nodes.rationale: Measured false: 60 MB survived compaction and survives every future compaction, because preserving the live tree is what compaction is for.
nodes.norm_label: rejected: doing nothing because compaction bounds the repository

nodes.label: A failed or refused delete is not retried every cycle
nodes.rationale: The trap ADR 0005 hit: a maintenance condition that stays true after a failure turns into a wasted network call on every poll, forever. Reaping also logs at warn, naming the peer, object count and bytes, because a destructive unattended action has to be visible in ddrop logs.
nodes.norm_label: a failed or refused delete is not retried every cycle

nodes.label: dead-drop architecture overview
nodes.rationale: Each layer only knows about the one below it. The application never names a transport, and the transport never sees plaintext. Flow: application to Workspace over a local socket (or nothing at all in proxy mode), Workspace to mailbox engine to transport manager to adapters to the same stack on another machine.

nodes.label: @fyrlabs/dead-drop/protocol
nodes.rationale: Decides what a message is: envelope shape, framing, encryption, chunking, the error model. Zero dependencies, zero policy. Knows nothing about transports, workspaces or applications.

nodes.label: @fyrlabs/dead-drop-transport-sdk
nodes.rationale: The contract third-party adapters compile against. Deliberately tiny and deliberately stable: the only thing outside this repository that has to keep working across releases.

nodes.label: @fyrlabs/dead-drop/core
nodes.rationale: All policy: which transport carries a message, when to retry, when to give up, what to record. The mailbox engine and the transport manager live here.

nodes.label: @fyrlabs/dead-drop/runtime
nodes.rationale: Turns core into a product: workspaces, exposures, discovery, the control plane, plugin loading.

nodes.label: @fyrlabs/dead-drop/sdk and @fyrlabs/dead-drop front doors
nodes.rationale: The two public entry points applications use.

nodes.label: Workspace (request/response, pub/sub, RPC)
nodes.rationale: Top layer of the runtime, reached by the application over a local socket or directly in proxy mode. Knows only the mailbox engine below it.

nodes.label: Mailbox engine
nodes.rationale: Framing, chunking, ack, dedupe, redelivery and polling. Supplies the messaging semantics that store adapters do not have, so adapter authors do not each reimplement at-least-once delivery.

nodes.label: Transport manager
nodes.rationale: Scoring, retry, circuit breaker, failover and health. The boundary above which nothing may name a transport.

nodes.label: Adapters (filesystem, git, github, memory, third-party)
nodes.rationale: Sit below the transport manager and carry bytes to the same stack on another machine. They never see plaintext.

nodes.label: Nothing above the transport manager names a transport
nodes.rationale: The rule that keeps the layering honest. Application code cannot ask for 'the GitHub one'; if it could, transport independence would be a slogan rather than a property. The same reasoning forbids anything above the manager from reading policy.mode.
nodes.norm_label: nothing above the transport manager names a transport

nodes.label: store transport kind
nodes.rationale: put, get, list, delete, optionally watch. Around 50 lines for a typical backend; the mailbox engine supplies the messaging semantics. Chosen because nearly everything people want to use (GitHub, GitLab, OneDrive, SharePoint, S3, Dropbox, a synced folder) is an object store with no delivery semantics, and making every adapter author reimplement polling, acknowledgement, deduplication and at-least-once delivery would put subtle bugs in someone else's package.

nodes.label: native transport kind
nodes.rationale: The backend already is a message system: it sends and subscribes directly.

nodes.label: ADR 0001 (store and native transports)
nodes.rationale: Records why the original sketch, in which every adapter implements send, receive and acknowledgement, was the wrong shape and was changed.

nodes.label: Mailbox key layout
nodes.rationale: ws/<workspace>/inbox/<peer>/<messageId>.ddf for direct messages, topic/<channel>/<messageId>.ddf for broadcast, peers/<peer>.ddf for presence beacons, dead/<peer>/<messageId>.ddf for dead letters. Keys are readable, and time-sortable ids give rough FIFO for free.

nodes.label: Delete is the acknowledgement
nodes.rationale: Sending is a write; receiving is list, fetch, decode, hand to a handler, delete. That single choice is what gives at-least-once delivery over a store that has no concept of a message.

nodes.label: Broadcast retention reaper and subscriber cursors
nodes.rationale: Broadcast messages belong to every subscriber so nobody may delete them; subscribers keep a local cursor and ask for keys after it, and a retention reaper removes messages past the window. It takes age from the message id rather than the store's modification time, because plenty of backends do not report one and treating 'age unknown' as 'old enough to delete' would destroy messages other subscribers had not read.
nodes.norm_label: broadcast retention reaper and subscriber cursors

nodes.label: Adaptive polling with watch interrupt
nodes.rationale: Speeds up to the minimum interval while traffic flows and backs off to the maximum when idle; a transport supporting watch interrupts the wait instead of polling at all. Polling a rate-limited API every 250ms forever is how a transport gets throttled.

nodes.label: Transport scoring (health 45, reliability 25, latency 20, rate-limit headroom 10)
nodes.rationale: Every transport is scored 0..1. An open circuit breaker scores zero, so it is chosen only when nothing else exists.
nodes.norm_label: transport scoring (health 45, reliability 25, latency 20, rate-limit headroom 10)

nodes.label: Circuit breaker
nodes.rationale: An open breaker forces a transport's score to zero rather than removing it outright, so it remains a last resort.

nodes.label: Retry with jittered backoff, then failover
nodes.rationale: An operation is retried on its chosen transport with exponential backoff and full jitter, then moved to the next. Failover is skipped for caller-side errors, which fail identically everywhere.
nodes.norm_label: retry with jittered backoff, then failover

nodes.label: Policy modes: score, failover, parallel
nodes.rationale: score is the default and the healthiest wins; failover respects the operator's declared order even when it is objectively slower; parallel writes through everything, made safe by receiver deduplication.

nodes.label: runWrite single write entry point
nodes.rationale: How many transports carry a write is a policy question, so callers ask the manager for a write rather than choosing between one transport and all of them. Nothing above the manager reads policy.mode, for the same reason nothing above it names a transport.

nodes.label: Selection governs writes only
nodes.rationale: The mailbox polls every store transport each cycle, and so do discovery and queue depth, so a message is found wherever it was written.

nodes.label: Request/response correlation
nodes.rationale: The runtime owns correlation. A request registers a pending promise keyed by its message id, sets a TTL equal to its timeout so it cannot outlive the caller's patience, and sends; the remote handler produces a response envelope carrying correlationId, which resolves the promise. A late response to a timed-out request is logged at debug and dropped, because that is normal, not an error.

nodes.label: Structured DeadDropError in responses
nodes.rationale: Handler failures are marshalled into the response as a structured error, so NOT_FOUND for a missing channel and SERVICE_ERROR for a handler that threw arrive as distinguishable errors rather than strings to match on.

nodes.label: Proxy mode (ddrop expose / ddrop connect)
nodes.rationale: ddrop expose --target http://localhost:3000 --name my-api registers a handler on channel http/my-api; ddrop connect peer/my-api starts a local HTTP server that packs each request into an envelope, waits for the response, and unpacks it.

nodes.label: Length-prefixed JSON head with raw byte body
nodes.rationale: HTTP bodies travel as raw bytes after a length-prefixed JSON head rather than base64 inside it, so proxying a 10 MB response costs 10 MB, not 13 MB.
nodes.norm_label: length-prefixed json head with raw byte body

nodes.label: Observability at the runtime/transport boundary
nodes.rationale: Structured JSON logs with credential redaction by field name and by value pattern; counters, gauges and histograms with Prometheus text output and no client-library dependency; spans in a bounded ring buffer so ddrop can answer 'which hop was slow' without an external collector. Living at the boundary is what gives an application transport latency, retries, failovers and payload sizes without instrumenting anything.

nodes.label: One runtime per machine
nodes.rationale: Polling is the scarce resource. A process per project multiplies requests against the same rate limits for no benefit. One runtime hosts many workspaces, each with its own keys, transports, mailbox and peer identity, sharing only the process and the log.

nodes.label: Request timeout bounds the whole request (since 0.3.0)
nodes.norm_label: request timeout bounds the whole request (since 0.3.0)

nodes.label: Per-message TTL in the encrypted header
nodes.norm_label: per-message ttl in the encrypted header

nodes.label: workDir single-writer ownership and peer clones
nodes.norm_label: workdir single-writer ownership and peer clones

nodes.label: Data branch compaction with compare-and-swap lease
nodes.norm_label: data branch compaction with compare-and-swap lease

nodes.label: Authentication delegated to gh (no token seen)
nodes.norm_label: authentication delegated to gh (no token seen)

nodes.norm_label: github does not forward pushretries/author identity

nodes.norm_label: worked example: lan folder with github behind it

nodes.norm_label: messages stay on the transport they were written to

nodes.norm_label: static exposure limits (get/head, 32 mib, clamped paths)

nodes.norm_label: allowpeers is a guardrail, not a security boundary

nodes.label: ADR 0004: dashboard binds TCP and holds no runtime
nodes.norm_label: adr 0004: dashboard binds tcp and holds no runtime

nodes.label: Poisoned message never blocks the queue head
nodes.norm_label: poisoned message never blocks the queue head

nodes.norm_label: broadcast subscribers get no retry (cursor moved on)

nodes.label: Startup does not depend on a reachable transport
nodes.norm_label: startup does not depend on a reachable transport

nodes.norm_label: one beacon in flight, abandoned past the expiry window
