nodes.norm_label: queue depth read from object keys alone

nodes.label: Trace id equals the message id
nodes.norm_label: trace id equals the message id

nodes.label: Troubleshooting: cannot reach the runtime control socket
nodes.norm_label: troubleshooting: cannot reach the runtime control socket

nodes.label: Workspace name is an HKDF salt
nodes.norm_label: workspace name is an hkdf salt

nodes.label: refusing unencrypted frame on an encrypted workspace
nodes.norm_label: refusing unencrypted frame on an encrypted workspace

nodes.label: no workspace key matches key id
nodes.norm_label: no workspace key matches key id

nodes.label: Back up the workspace secret, not the store
nodes.norm_label: back up the workspace secret, not the store

nodes.label: Authorise on identity, never on from
nodes.norm_label: authorise on identity, never on from

nodes.label: Two-package split keeps the transport contract standalone
nodes.norm_label: two-package split keeps the transport contract standalone

nodes.label: Client talks to a running runtime over the control socket
nodes.norm_label: client talks to a running runtime over the control socket

nodes.label: Identity is a shared secret
nodes.rationale: A workspace has one 32-byte secret and possession of it is membership. There is no per-peer identity and no signing key, so `from` in an envelope is a claim rather than an assertion. Deliberate simplification: per-peer keypairs and signed envelopes would be a protocol change, not a configuration change.

nodes.label: 32-byte workspace secret
nodes.rationale: 32 random bytes from crypto.randomBytes, printed as ddk1_<base64url>. Holding it is membership, so it is treated like a password.

nodes.label: Threat: any member can impersonate any member
nodes.rationale: Accepted consequence of the shared-secret identity: nothing binds a peer name to a key.
nodes.norm_label: threat: any member can impersonate any member

nodes.label: Threat: any member reads every message
nodes.rationale: One key decrypts every inbox in the workspace, including mail addressed to other peers.
nodes.norm_label: threat: any member reads every message

nodes.label: Threat: any member deletes every message
nodes.rationale: Authorisation over the store belongs to the transport, not to dead-drop, so dead-drop cannot bound delete.
nodes.norm_label: threat: any member deletes every message

nodes.label: Revocation only by rotating the secret
nodes.rationale: Removing a peer means rotating the secret for everybody; nothing else revokes access.
nodes.norm_label: revocation only by rotating the secret

nodes.label: Per-peer keypairs and signed envelopes (not built)
nodes.rationale: What would be needed for send-but-not-read peers or an audit trail surviving a malicious member. Explicitly out of scope for the shipping protocol.
nodes.norm_label: per-peer keypairs and signed envelopes (not built)

nodes.label: ADR 0007: per-peer key wrapping
nodes.rationale: Proposes making the shared secret an enrollment token and wrapping a per-era data key to each peer's X25519 public key, so admitting a peer stops handing over the key to everything already written and removing one stops forcing a workspace-wide re-key. Proposed, not implemented.

nodes.label: Transport treated as hostile storage
nodes.rationale: A GitHub repository, synced folder or S3 bucket may be readable by people outside the workspace, so nothing confidential may rely on store access control.

nodes.label: Whole envelope encrypted
nodes.rationale: Payload, channel, from, to, headers, correlation ids and content type all sit inside AES-256-GCM ciphertext.

nodes.label: Frame preamble: authenticated, not encrypted
nodes.rationale: Frame magic, flags byte and key id stay in clear text but are the AEAD additional authenticated data, so tampering fails decryption.

nodes.label: Documented leak: unprotected metadata
nodes.rationale: Object keys, message sizes/counts/timing, and which peers exist and when they are active are visible to anyone who can read the store.

nodes.label: Cleartext object key layout
nodes.rationale: ws/<workspace>/inbox/<peer>/<messageId>.ddf exposes workspace names, peer names and broadcast channel names in clear text.

nodes.label: Leak: sizes, counts and timing
nodes.rationale: Traffic analysis is unmitigated; no padding or cover traffic exists.

nodes.label: Leak: peer existence and activity
nodes.rationale: Presence is inferable from the store without any key.

nodes.label: Readable keys are on purpose
nodes.rationale: When the transport is a git repo or a folder a human has to operate, being able to look at it and understand it is worth more than the metadata it costs. If that trade is wrong, use a transport with a private backing store.

nodes.label: HKDF-SHA256 key derivation
nodes.rationale: Salt is the workspace name, info is dead-drop/v1/workspace-aead. Salting by name means the same secret in two differently-named workspaces yields unrelated keys, so a frame cannot be replayed across workspaces.

nodes.label: AES-256-GCM with per-frame random IV
nodes.rationale: Fresh random 96-bit IV per frame; the frame preamble is the additional authenticated data.

nodes.label: Key id (8 hex of SHA-256)
nodes.rationale: Not secret; it exists only so a receiver can pick the right key during a rotation.

nodes.label: Two-stage key rotation
nodes.rationale: Frames name the key they were sealed with, so both keys can be accepted at once. Add the new secret second everywhere, then swap the order, then drop the old after the longest plausible in-flight TTL. Skipping the accept-both step breaks every peer not yet updated.

nodes.label: Where secrets live
nodes.rationale: Four negative rules: not in the config file, not in application processes, not in logs, not in printed git remote urls.

nodes.label: ${env:NAME} config expansion
nodes.rationale: ddrop init writes "${env:DEADDROP_SECRET}" and the parser expands it at load time, so the real value stays in a secret manager or the shell environment.

nodes.label: Credentials stay in the runtime
nodes.rationale: Applications talk to the runtime over a local socket; transport credentials and workspace secrets never enter application processes.

nodes.label: Logger redaction
nodes.rationale: Redacts by field name (token, secret, authorization) and by pattern (ddk1_, ghp_, glpat-, AWS key ids, Slack tokens), including inside message text and nested objects.

nodes.label: Inline credential stripping from git urls
nodes.rationale: Credentials embedded in a remote url are stripped before any error reaches a log.
nodes.norm_label: inline credential stripping from git urls

nodes.label: Control plane on a 0600 Unix socket
nodes.rationale: Never localhost TCP: a TCP port is reachable by every process on the machine, every container sharing the network namespace, and sometimes from outside, while a socket file is governed by filesystem permissions. Anything that can talk to the control plane can publish, call any peer and read runtime state, so it is the door to the whole workspace.
nodes.norm_label: control plane on a 0600 unix socket

nodes.label: Exposures and workspace-wide reach
nodes.rationale: ddrop expose makes a local server reachable by every peer; there is no per-request authentication beyond workspace membership.

nodes.label: allowPeers is organisational, not a boundary
nodes.rationale: Peer names are self-asserted under the shared-secret identity, so restricting an exposure to named peers is an organisational control only.
nodes.norm_label: allowpeers is organisational, not a boundary

nodes.label: Static exposure traversal rejection
nodes.rationale: Every path resolves inside the configured root; percent-encoded .., absolute paths and null bytes are handled.

nodes.label: Proxy hop-by-hop stripping and no redirect following
nodes.norm_label: proxy hop-by-hop stripping and no redirect following

nodes.label: Denial-of-service bounds
nodes.rationale: The transport is shared and a peer can be malicious or broken, so every accepted size is bounded: 64 MiB decoded and decompressed frames, 64 MiB / 256 chunk groups, 32 MiB HTTP bodies, 1 MiB control-plane bodies, 10 000 dedupe entries for an hour.

nodes.label: Gzip bomb fails as PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE
nodes.rationale: Decompressed size is enforced by zlib rather than discovered by exhausting memory.

nodes.label: Undecodable objects are deleted
nodes.rationale: Prevents a poison object being re-read forever.

nodes.label: Reaping another peer's mail
nodes.rationale: Only a recipient empties its own inbox, so mail for a peer that never returns is storage nothing reclaims. Peers delete mail older than inboxOrphanMs with no presence beacon (or a beacon older than the window). This grants no new privilege, since every member could already read and delete any inbox; what changes is that correct peers now delete data they did not author, so the risk to weigh is accidental loss. Deciding costs a listing only: age is read from the message id in the key, nothing is downloaded or decrypted, and a real TTL is unreadable from outside.

nodes.label: inboxOrphanMs setting
nodes.rationale: 7 days by default; 0 disables reaping. A peer offline longer than the window loses its mail.

nodes.label: Replay defence
nodes.rationale: Unique message ids plus a dedupe store that persists across restarts drop a replayed frame. Requests are stamped with a TTL equal to their timeout, so a captured request cannot be usefully replayed after expiry. A member replaying their own traffic inside the TTL is not defended, because they could simply send the message again.

nodes.label: DedupeStore
nodes.rationale: Bounded at 10 000 entries for one hour and persisted, so it serves both DoS bounding and replay defence.

nodes.label: Private security reporting
nodes.rationale: Issues go to the repository owner privately rather than the public tracker.

nodes.label: The problem: the network is the obstacle
nodes.rationale: A laptop behind NAT, a locked-down corporate environment, a CI runner, an air-gapped review box that can still reach a git remote. The usual answer is deploying a broker, tunnel or relay, and the deployment costs more than the problem.
nodes.norm_label: the problem: the network is the obstacle

nodes.label: Existing shared infrastructure becomes the transport
nodes.rationale: Two machines almost always already share a git repository, synced folder, object store or wiki: infrastructure that exists, is already authenticated, and is already allowed through the firewall.
nodes.norm_label: existing shared infrastructure becomes the transport

nodes.label: Transport is an implementation detail
nodes.rationale: Applications talk only to their local runtime, so swapping GitHub for a shared folder is a config change. Nothing above the transport manager may name a transport, because if it could, transport independence would be a slogan rather than a property.

nodes.label: Delivery is implemented once
nodes.rationale: Most wanted backends are object stores with no delivery semantics. Asking every adapter author to reinvent polling, acknowledgement, deduplication and redelivery would produce a dozen subtly different sets of delivery bugs in packages the project does not control, so a store adapter implements four methods and the runtime supplies the rest.

nodes.label: Existing applications should not have to change
nodes.rationale: Proxy mode exposes a server that has no idea dead-drop exists. The SDK is for applications that want more, not a tax on applications that want less.
nodes.norm_label: existing applications should not have to change

nodes.label: Say what is true
nodes.rationale: At-least-once delivery and best-effort per-recipient ordering are stated plainly in guarantees.md rather than buried, and the security model says what is not protected as clearly as what is.

nodes.label: What exists today
nodes.rationale: Four transports (filesystem, git, github, memory), encryption, chunking, compression, retries, circuit breaking, failover, deduplication, health-based routing, structured logs, Prometheus metrics, tracing, proxy mode, static exposures, and a plugin contract stable enough for third parties.

nodes.label: Roadmap: more transports as separate packages
nodes.rationale: S3-compatible storage, OneDrive and SharePoint are the gaps. GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps already work through the git transport by remote url and earn dedicated packages only if their APIs offer something git does not.
nodes.norm_label: roadmap: more transports as separate packages

nodes.label: Roadmap: a token path for GitHub
nodes.rationale: Authentication is delegated entirely to gh today; a REST path behind the existing GhClient seam would remove that dependency where installing gh is the hard part.
nodes.norm_label: roadmap: a token path for github

nodes.label: Roadmap: streaming large payloads
nodes.rationale: A response is buffered whole today and capped at 32 MiB.

nodes.label: Roadmap: a plugin ecosystem
nodes.rationale: The measure of success is a transport written by someone who has never read this repository's internals, passing the conformance suite on the first try.

nodes.label: Non-goal: not a message broker
nodes.rationale: A round trip over a git remote costs seconds, not milliseconds. If you have Kafka, use Kafka. This targets the case where standing up infrastructure is the expensive part, not throughput.

nodes.label: Non-goal: not a way around your security policy
nodes.rationale: Data moves only through channels you are already authorised to use; features whose main purpose would be evading controls are rejected.
nodes.norm_label: non-goal: not a way around your security policy

nodes.label: Non-goal: not a service mesh
nodes.rationale: No competition with Kubernetes, no service discovery at scale, no sidecars.

nodes.label: Non-goal: not a database
nodes.rationale: The transport holds messages in flight, with retention and a reaper. It is not storage to query.

nodes.label: History: the rejected send/receive/acknowledge interface
nodes.rationale: An earlier sketch specified one send/receive/acknowledge transport interface; implementation showed it was the wrong shape for the target backends and it became the two-kind contract.

nodes.label: A transport is an ordinary npm package
nodes.rationale: No fork, no pull request, nothing merged upstream: publish it, npm install it, name it in a config file. Convention is <scope>/deaddrop-transport-<name>, and local paths work for development.
nodes.norm_label: a transport is an ordinary npm package

nodes.label: defineTransport
nodes.rationale: Entry point from @fyrlabs/dead-drop-transport-sdk taking id, capabilities, parseConfig and create.

nodes.label: Declared capabilities
nodes.rationale: kind, ordering, binaryPayloads, delete, watch, orderedList, maxPayloadBytes. The conformance suite adapts to what you declare, and declaring a capability you do not have will fail.

nodes.label: parseConfig
nodes.rationale: Throws DeadDropError('CONFIG_INVALID') at start-up so a typo fails immediately rather than at 3am, with a message that says how to fix it.

nodes.label: StoreTransport interface
nodes.rationale: put, get, list, delete, optional watch, plus health and close. Four required methods; dead-drop supplies framing, encryption, chunking, acknowledgement, retries with jitter, deduplication, dead-lettering, health-based routing, failover, metrics and tracing.

nodes.label: Rule: get on a missing key resolves undefined
nodes.rationale: Absence is normal: another consumer may have deleted the object between the list and the get, so it must never throw for absence.
nodes.norm_label: rule: get on a missing key resolves undefined

nodes.label: Rule: delete is idempotent
nodes.rationale: Deleting a key that does not exist must succeed, because concurrent consumers race on the same key.

nodes.label: Rule: put is durable when it resolves
nodes.rationale: If the backend batches, resolve after the batch lands, not when it is queued, or at-least-once delivery is silently broken.
nodes.norm_label: rule: put is durable when it resolves

nodes.label: Rule: list matches on path boundaries
nodes.rationale: inbox/peer-a must not return inbox/peer-abc/..., or one peer reads another's inbox by prefix accident.
nodes.norm_label: rule: list matches on path boundaries

nodes.label: Rule: put with ifAbsent is atomic create-or-fail
nodes.rationale: Use the backend's create-or-fail primitive; a check-then-write race defeats the purpose.
nodes.norm_label: rule: put with ifabsent is atomic create-or-fail

nodes.label: assertValidKey / assertValidPrefix
nodes.rationale: Call before interpolating a key into a path or URL; the conformance suite checks that you do.

nodes.label: Rule: concurrency is expected
nodes.rationale: Two calls can be in flight at once.

nodes.label: startAfter in ListOptions
nodes.rationale: Subscribers use it to ask what is new since a key, which on a remote backend is the difference between one cheap call and one that grows with retention.

nodes.label: health() and TransportHealth

nodes.rationale: The code decides what happens next. TRANSPORT_ERROR and TIMEOUT retry then fail over; RATE_LIMITED retries and honours retryAfterMs exactly instead of guessing; UNAUTHORIZED, BAD_REQUEST, PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE and UNSUPPORTED are not failed over because they fail the same way on every backend; CANCELLED is neither retried nor counted against the circuit breaker.

nodes.label: registerConformanceTests
nodes.rationale: Framework-agnostic: returns plain { name, run } cases so it works with vitest, node:test, jest or a bare script and pulls no test runner into the dependency tree. settleMs is non-zero only for eventually consistent backends.

nodes.label: Native transports (kind: 'native')

nodes.label: Third-party credential and log hygiene

nodes.label: maxPayloadBytes and chunk sizing
nodes.rationale: dead-drop chunks to this number, so an inaccurate value produces frames the backend rejects.
